cards.text: Paul is writing to the churches in Galatia, and he's telling them about something that happened. Cephas, also called Peter, one of Jesus' apostles, comes to the city of Antioch. Grab a seat, friend, because this one gets AWKWARD.

cards.question: When Cephas comes to Antioch, what does Paul do?

cards.text: Not a long sigh, not a vague post online, TO HIS FACE. Paul says Cephas stood condemned, so let's back up and see why.
Here's the backstory. Before certain men came from James, one of the leaders in Jerusalem, Cephas had a regular habit at mealtime.

cards.question: Before the men from James came, Cephas used to eat with the ___.

cards.text: Then the men from James arrive, and Cephas starts to draw back and separate himself. It's like the coworker laughing at all your jokes until the boss walks in, and suddenly he is VERY interested in his phone.

cards.question: Why does Cephas pull away from the Gentiles once the men from James arrive?

answers.text: He was afraid of the circumcision group
He was angry with the Gentiles
He was called back to Jerusalem

cards.text: And Cephas isn't the only one. The other Jews join him.

cards.question: Paul calls what Cephas and the other Jews are doing ___.
Barnabas, Paul's own partner in ministry, stays out of it.

cards.text: EVEN BARNABAS, friend. When Paul sees they're not walking in line with the truth of the gospel, he speaks up to Cephas.

cards.question: Paul pulls Cephas aside and talks to him privately.

cards.text: In front of them all, Paul asks him, “If you, who are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?” Friend, that is NOT the kind of question you want to hear with everybody watching.

cards.question: What is Paul pointing out with his question to Cephas?

answers.text: He lives like a Gentile but pushes Gentiles to live like Jews
He never once sat down to eat with any Gentiles
He should never have come to Antioch at all

cards.text: Then Paul gets to the heart of it, starting with Jews by birth like himself. He says even they know something about how a person is justified.

cards.question: According to Paul, how is a person justified?

cards.text: So Paul says Jews like him have believed in Christ Jesus too, so they may be justified by faith in Christ. Friend, if trying harder could do it, I'd have stamped my way out of that junk drawer all by myself.

cards.question: Paul says that by works of the law, a few people will still be justified.

cards.text: Then Paul raises a hard question. If, while seeking to be justified in Christ, people are found to be sinners, does that make Christ a minister of sin?

cards.question: Paul asks whether that would make Christ a minister of sin. What's his answer?

cards.text: Then Paul pictures tearing something down and building it right back up. Like finally deleting the app that eats your whole evening, then downloading it again before bed.

cards.question: Paul says rebuilding what he already tore down would prove him to be a ___.

cards.text: Then Paul says something that sounds upside down. Through the law, he died to the law.

cards.question: Paul says dying to the law means he no longer lives for God.

cards.text: Then Paul gets personal. He says he has been crucified with Christ, and he no longer lives.

cards.question: Paul says he no longer lives, but ___ lives in him.

cards.text: Slow down here, friend. Paul says the life he lives in the body, he lives by faith in the Son of God.

cards.question: What does Paul say the Son of God did for him?

answers.text: Loved him and gave Himself up for him
Rewarded him for keeping the law well
Picked him for being the best apostle

cards.text: Paul wraps it up: he does not set aside the grace of God. Me neither, friend, that grace is the only reason I'm not still in the back of a drawer.

cards.question: Paul says if righteousness came through the law, Christ's death would still have a purpose.

findings.problem: The opening card states facts from outside the passage without references: that Paul is writing to the churches in Galatia (Gal 1:2) and that Cephas is also called Peter (John 1:42). The card cites only Galatians 2:11.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The passage opens mid-thought with "however" (2:11), which contrasts with 2:1-10. There, Cephas, James and John gave Paul the right hand of fellowship (2:9). The opening card doesn't give this context, so the baker misses why the clash in Antioch is surprising. The card spends its third sentence on a joke instead.

rule.text: If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: James is introduced as "one of the leaders in Jerusalem," a fact from outside the passage with no reference (for example Gal 2:9). The card cites only Galatians 2:12.

rule.text: Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: The question calls Barnabas "Paul's own partner in ministry," a fact from outside the passage with no reference (for example Gal 2:1, 9 or Acts 13:2). The card cites only Galatians 2:13.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: This card is a bare restatement of the verse ("And Cephas isn't the only one. The other Jews join him.") with almost none of Papa Dorin's voice.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Most story cards in this stop read as plain paraphrase with little of Papa Dorin's voice: card 1, card 5, card 9 and card 11. There are no loud moments, and the humor is limited to cards 3 and 7.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The question says "Paul asks whether that would make Christ a minister of sin." Here "that" points back to card 5, which is no longer on screen. The question should say what "that" is: being found to be sinners while seeking to be justified in Christ.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "Picked him for being the best apostle" reads as silly. Its tone doesn't match the other answers, so the right answer is easy to spot.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.
